\chapter{El Libro --- And a Word Made of Tree Bark}
\label{ch:noun-libro}
\hlchaptermodality{57}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say el libro and tengo un libro, and contrast it with la casa as a gender pair.}

Complete ES-C43-libro: produce el libro and tengo un libro, and say what Latin liber originally named.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el libro]{el libro — \textquotedblleft{}book\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C43-libro}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}the house.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{La casa}.) Why \emph{la} and not \emph{el}? (\emph{Casa} is feminine.) Here is one that goes the other way.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{r-tap} — a single flick of the tongue: \emph{LEE-broh}. One tap, not a roll.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{el libro} — \emph{the book}.
\end{quote}

Latin \textbf{liber} did not mean \textquotedblleft{}book.\textquotedblright{} It meant the \textbf{inner bark of a tree} — the thin, pale layer just under the rough outside, which is what Romans wrote on before they had anything better.

So the word travelled the way these words usually do: from the \textbf{material}, to the \textbf{thing made of it}, to the thing itself long after the material is gone. Nobody has written on bark for two thousand years, and the word has not noticed.

English took the same root and kept it in the places books live:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{library} — and French \emph{livre}, Italian \emph{libro}.
  \item \textbf{libretto} — Italian for \textquotedblleft{}little book,\textquotedblright{} the words of an opera.
\end{itemize}

English's own word went the same route from a different tree: \textbf{book} is related to \textbf{beech}, whose bark the Germanic peoples wrote on. Two languages, two trees, the same idea.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a masculine noun to sit beside the feminine one}]
\emph{Libro} ends in \emph{-o} and is masculine, so it takes \textbf{el}.

\begin{quote}
\emph{el libro} — the book. \emph{Tengo un libro.} — I have a book. \emph{la casa} — the house. \emph{Tengo una casa.} — I have a house.
\end{quote}

Two nouns, one of each gender, side by side. That pairing is worth more than either noun alone: from here on, when something in Spanish depends on gender, you have a plain example of both to test it against.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el libro\textquotedblright{} — one tap on the \emph{r}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Tengo un libro\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Tengo una casa\textquotedblright{} — hear the article follow the noun
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textquotedblleft{}The book\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{El libro}}.) \textquotedblleft{}The house\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{La casa}}.) What was \emph{liber} before it was a book? (Tree \textbf{bark}.) Next: a noun you can build yourself, out of a verb you already have.
\end{tcolorbox}
